Data collected from: <https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/> \
Original data from: <https://shakespeare.mit.edu/>

This dataset shows dialogue from 3 of Shakespeare's plays: *Hamlet*, *Macbeth*, and *Romeo and Juliet*. This project looks at how word usage differs between plays, which characters speak the most, and how frequently certain themes appear.

We want to answer the following questions:

1. Which characters speak the most in each play?
2. How frequently do words related to love and death appear?
3. Which words are most frequently used in each play?

## Loading data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

hamlet <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/hamlet.csv")

macbeth <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/macbeth.csv")

romeo_juliet <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/romeo_juliet.csv")

plays <- bind_rows(
  hamlet |> mutate(play = "Hamlet"),
  macbeth |> mutate(play = "Macbeth"),
  romeo_juliet |> mutate(play = "Romeo and Juliet")
)

plays <- plays |>
  filter(!is.na(dialogue), !is.na(character)) |>
  filter(!str_detect(character, regex("stage direction", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(
    dialogue = str_squish(dialogue),
    character = str_to_title(character),
    play = factor(play, levels = c("Hamlet", "Macbeth", "Romeo and Juliet")),
    word_count = str_count(dialogue, "\\b[A-Za-z]+\\b")
  )
```

## Which characters speak the most in each play?

This plot shows the total number of words spoken by each character.

```{r}
most_words <- plays |>
  group_by(play, character) |>
  summarise(
    total_words = sum(word_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(play) |>
  slice_max(total_words, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    character = fct_reorder(character, total_words)
  )

ggplot(most_words, aes(x = total_words/1000, y = character, fill = play)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~play, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Words spoken by main characters",
    x = "Total words spoken (thousands)",
    y = "Character"
  )
```

In *Hamlet*, Hamlet speaks the most, followed by King Claudius. In *Macbeth*, Macbeth and Lady Macbeth speaks the most, followed by Malcom. In *Romeo and Juliet*, Romeo and Juliet speak the most, followed by Friar Laurence. The abundance of Hamlet speaking in *Hamlet* tells us that the play is more centered towards its protagonist compared to the other 2 plays.


## How frequently do words related to love and death appear?

The plot shows the percentage of the text in the play that has words involving love or death. Matches for love include "love", "loved", "lover", and "lovers". Matches for death include "death", "dead", "die", "dies", "died", and "dying".

```{r}
love_death <- plays |>
  mutate(
    love = str_detect(
      dialogue,
      regex("\\blov(?=e\\b|ed\\b|er\\b|ers\\b)[a-z]+\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    death = str_detect(
      dialogue,
      regex("\\b(?:death|dead|die|dies|died|dying)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  )

love_death_counts <- love_death |>
  group_by(play) |>
  summarise(
    love_percent = mean(love) * 100,
    death_percent = mean(death) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(love_percent, death_percent),
    names_to = "theme",
    values_to = "percentage"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    theme = recode(
      theme,
      love_percent = "Love",
      death_percent = "Death"
    )
  )

ggplot(love_death_counts, aes(x = play, y = percentage, fill = theme)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Percentage of dialogue entries mentioning love or death",
    x = "Play",
    y = "Dialogue entries containing love or death (%)",
    fill = "Theme"
  ) 
```

From the graph, we can see that *Romeo and Juliet* have much more references to love and death compared to Shakespeare's other works, which makes sense, as the main cast loved each other and died. Both *Romeo and Juliet* and *Hamlet* have similar levels of love and death mentioned, while *Macbeth* mentions love a lot more than death, hinting that it's probably more of a light-hearted play compared to the other two. 

## Which words are most frequently used in each play?

The plot shows the top 10 most used words and how much they are used. To prevent the graph from displaying words like "the", "and", "to", and "i", the plot will only display words that are at least 7 characters long.
```{r}
common_words <- plays |>
  mutate(
    word = str_to_lower(dialogue),
    word = str_extract_all(word, "\\b[a-z]+\\b")
  ) |>
  unnest(word) |>
  filter(str_length(word) >= 7) |>
  count(play, word, sort = TRUE) |>
  group_by(play) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(common_words, aes(x = n, y = reorder(word, n), fill = play)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~play, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequently used words in each play",
    x = "Word frequency",
    y = "Word"
  )
```

The word 'nothing' is used a lot in both *Hamlet* and *Macbeth*. Aside from names, the word 'madness' is mentioned a lot in *Hamlet*, hinting at a character that's insane consistently throughout the story. 'Against' and 'strange' is consistently mentioned in *Macbeth*, and 'farewell' in *Romeo and Juliet*. It can then be inferred that there are lots of farewells throughout the plot of *Romeo and Juliet*. Judging by only the most common words, it can be assumed that *Hamlet* takes place in either Denmark or England (perhaps there is a conflict between the two) and *Macbeth* takes place in Scotland.
